title: Expanding Your Options
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This entry addresses a common decision-making trap: settling on the first workable option and spending energy justifying it rather than generating a fuller set of choices. It offers three reframing questions to surface hidden options — imagining what a rival or admired peer would do, reverse-engineering a guaranteed failure and inverting it, and asking what you'd do if none of the current options were available. Each question is meant to interrupt default thinking patterns and reveal choices that weren't obvious at first glance. The piece frames a richer option set as the real driver of decision quality.
points: A small option set leads to inferior decisions; leaders often grab the first idea and justify it.
Three reframing questions can surface hidden options: 'What would X do,' reverse brainstorming a failure, and imagining none of the current choices were available.
Shifting perspective is the mechanism that unlocks options beyond the obvious default set.
More and better options increase the odds of landing on a genuinely strong decision.
quotes: Studies show that leaders and decision-makers too often grab the first idea and then spend their energy justifying it.
An expanded list of options creates clarity and increases the odds that a leader will eventually land on a great choice.
Hidden options usually appear when decision-makers deliberately change how they look at a problem or opportunity.
The question to ask is: What would X do? — where X is a rival, an industry competitor, an admired stakeholder, or an experienced colleague.
By identifying the opposite course of action to a failed outcome, new and unusual options commonly emerge.
The more choices a leader considers, the better their thinking becomes.
